items.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I played the background, I played the soundtrack, then they had Marshall Royal come in and simulate what I was playing.

ctx.x: Yeah, right, for the shorts. And they had decided, the company decided, that they didn’t want me filmed on it because they’re going to try to sell them, Soundies—the shorts—down south, so they needed a black guy. So I played the background, I played the soundtrack, then they had Marshall Royal come in and simulate what I was playing. The whole thing was stupid because Marshall Royal looked more white than I did. So the whole thing didn’t make any sense.
How did Basie feel about it, did he take any position either way?

items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: I went to his band primarily as a clarinet player, because I was replacing Buddy De Franco

ctx.x: You don't get much (inaudible), do you?

No, nobody writes for a clarinet. So if you don't write for it, you don't play it. But that was pretty well my favorite instrument. As a matter of fact, when I went to work with the Basie Band in '51, when I went -- that was January, 1951 -- I went to his band primarily as a clarinet player, because I was replacing Buddy De Franco, who was an excellent clarinet player, one of the best jazz clarinet players there ever was. So, in replacing him, Basie was kind enough to remember that I was an exceptional player. So…

of the other two horns was extremely perilous. Clark Terry was playing the trumpet and Wardell Grey (PHONETIC) was playing the tenor saxophone and if you couldn't play, you just as well go home with them.
